pr.title: feat(adapter-neo4j): answer searches with one native ranked subgraph query
pr.body:
## Intent Neo4j's default search path answers with one native ranked subgraph: option A2 from the Neo4j native search report (data/docket-neo4j-native-search/report.md, under the Firstmate home), the second PR of option A after A1 (adapter subgraphs reach docket_search, merged as https://github.com/chrisjowen/docket/pull/47). A2 removes the per-hit N+1 queries and makes graph-native ranking the default without a model. "We need to initialise neo too": the integration test target is a real local Neo4j (the report's decision 2, option a), not only unit tests with a fake port. What the report's A2 (its proposal N2) asks for: replace the Neo4j adapter's default no-model search path - today one full-text query plus one extra neighbour query per hit (N+1), each neighbourhood flattened into a detail string, answered as entities and passages only with no graph block - with one deterministic, adapter-authored Cypher query and no model involved: full-text seeds from the memory_text index in the instance's scope, then a bounded 1-2 hop typed expansion from each seed, ranked by Lucene score times path confidence (the product of the relationships' stored confidence), with hub damping (dividing by the log of the end node's degree) so the best-connected nodes do not dominate, and per-seed caps on paths. It returns, through the adapter's existing answer machinery: an entities block of the seeds with their Lucene scores; a graph block of the path nodes, the edges in their stored direction each citing its evidence, and the ordered paths; a passages block of relevant excerpts as today; and one derived-fact evidence item per path as its "why", e.g. `orders -depends_on-> ledger (0.95, code+manifest) -depends_on-> ledger-db (0.9, runtime)`. Coverage stays top-k. Neighbours are context in the graph, not hits, keeping the existing concern that well-connected documents would otherwise come back for every query. Config knobs `traverse: { hops (up to 2-3), minConfidence, rels? }`, defaulting to all relationship types; direction is reported faithfully per edge. No contract change and no core change are required (A1 already makes adapter graph blocks visible in docket_search). Because the query is adapter-authored, the scope guard that covers only model-written Cypher does not cover it, so a unit test must check every node pattern carries $scope. One round trip instead of 1 + N per search. Ranking quality is a judgement call, so hops and minConfidence stay configurable. Integration tests run against a real Neo4j through NEO4J_TEST_URL. ## What Changed - The Neo4j adapter's no-model search (and the fallback when generated Cypher fails or finds nothing) no longer runs a full-text query plus one neighbour query per hit. It now runs one adapter-authored Cypher query in a timed read transaction (new `subgraph-search.ts`). The query takes full-text seeds from `memory_text` in the instance's scope and expands each seed by 1–3 hops in either direction, with every node checked against `$scope`. Paths are ranked by the product of their relationships' confidence, divided by the log of the end node's degree, and each seed keeps its best 3 paths. A path that another kept path extends is dropped. - `answer()` now returns four kinds of block: an entities block of the seeds with their Lucene scores; a graph block of the path nodes and edges, each edge in its stored direction and citing its evidence; passages as before; and one `derived-fact` evidence item per path explaining why it holds. The reached neighbours are graph context, not hits. `search()` hits now describe their paths in `detail`. The old `describeNeighbours` helper is removed. - A new optional `traverse: { hops (1–3, default 2), minConfidence (0–1, default 0), rels? }` config is validated in `config.ts`. Unit tests check that every node pattern in the query carries `$scope` and that only a whole hop count is written into it. They also cover path pruning and the answer blocks. The integration tests run against a real Neo4j through `NEO4J_TEST_URL` and cover the traversal reach and the ranking. The READMEs and the bundled `wheelhouse/docket` adapter `dist` are updated to match. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) ## Risk Assessment ⚠️ Medium: The change matches the A2 intent and is well tested against a real Neo4j, but the new default query lists every path before capping, runs with no timeout or deadline, and can be slow on dense graphs. ## Testing I stood up a throwaway Neo4j container, rebuilt the workspace, and ran the adapter's integration and unit tests against it (all pass). I then drove the real `docket` CLI and the `docket open` UI on a temp copy of the acme-platform example. Instrumenting the driver showed each search makes exactly one read query (after the one-off schema setup at startup), in a transaction capped at the request's remaining time. The answer carries the seeds' Lucene scores, directed edges with confidence that cite their paths, ordered paths, passages, and a derived fact per path. hops, rels and minConfidence change the result, and hops > 3 is rejected. Another scope's data never appears, even with a forced cross-scope relationship. UI screenshots show the graph block rendering. walkthrough.headline: The Neo4j adapter now answers model-less searches with one adapter-authored Cypher query that seeds from full-text match and expands 1-3 hops, instead of one full-text query plus a per-hit neighbour query.
walkthrough.what: The old path ran a full-text search then, for every hit, a separate neighbour query (N+1 round trips) and flattened each neighbourhood into a text blurb. take: This PR replaces a plain full-text search with one native Cypher query that returns ranked matches plus their best paths, and reshapes the Neo4j adapter to consume it. The core query (`subgraphQuery`) is inherently dense because it's Cypher doing full-text + traversal + ranking in one shot, but the TypeScript parsing/shaping layer around it (`subgraph-search.ts`) has a few spots that mix jobs or repeat the same small pattern that would read better as a named helper.

`neo4j-projection.ts` is a reasonably mechanical rewire (old full-text helpers swapped for the new subgraph ones), but the `timeLeft` closure introduced in `answer()` is slightly confusing: it's named like a pure getter yet also throws, and is called twice for two different purposes.

findings.title: `matchesOf` does parsing, dedup, ranking-filter and truncation all inline
findings.body: In one `.map` callback this function: parses raw path objects into `MatchPath`s, filters out non-simple (repeated-node) paths, filters out paths that another path extends, truncates to `PATHS_PER_MATCH`, and reshapes the row's scalar fields. Each step is a different concern and none is named, so a reader has to mentally label `all` → `simple` → `paths` to follow the pipeline. It works, but it's the kind of function where a future change (e.g. changing the extends-filter) risks touching unrelated parsing code by accident.
findings.suggestion: Pull the simple-path filter and the extends-filter into two named functions (e.g. `simplePaths`, `bestPaths`) so `matchesOf` just orchestrates parse → bestPaths → shape.

findings.title: Same optional-field spread idiom repeated four times
findings.body: `pathNode` (109-111), `pathEdge` (120), and the row-shaping in `matchesOf` (143-145) all repeat `...(x !== undefined ? { x } : {})` to conditionally include an optional key. It's not wrong, but it's duplicated boilerplate that obscures the actual shape being built, and any future optional field will copy the same pattern again.
findings.suggestion: Extract a small `optional(key, value)` helper that returns `{}` or `{ [key]: value }` and spread that instead.

findings.title: `timeLeft` closure both computes and enforces a deadline, and is called twice for different reasons
findings.body: `timeLeft` reads like a getter but also throws on expiry — the name doesn't signal the side effect. It's called once up front to get `timeoutMs` for the Cypher attempt, and again later (line 228) to re-check the deadline before the subgraph query. That's a reasonable intent (re-check after the Cypher attempt may have eaten the budget), but nothing in the code says that's why it's called twice, so a reader may think it's redundant or a copy-paste leftover.
findings.suggestion: Rename to something like `remainingOrThrow` and add a one-line comment at the second call site saying it re-checks the deadline after the Cypher attempt.

findings.title: `describePath` packs arrow-formatting and support-annotation into one dense chained expression
findings.body: The function is well-commented and small, but the body is a single `.map(...).join('')` with a nested ternary for arrow direction and an inline array-build for the `(confidence, sources)` suffix. It's readable once you've read the comment, but someone changing the support-string format has to parse the whole expression at once.
findings.suggestion: Split the per-node formatting into a small named step (e.g. a `supportSuffix(edge)` helper) to separate arrow logic from annotation logic.

findings.title: `pathEdge`'s confidence validation is buried in a spread condition

take: This is the heart of the PR: one Cypher query does full-text seeding, 1-3 hop expansion, hub-damped ranking, and per-match path limiting, then TypeScript post-processes the rows into paths, matches, and finally an answer with budget-bounded evidence.

The riskiest part isn't the ranking math, it's the scope guard: the pattern match `(seed)-[*1..hops]-(reached {scope: $scope})` only constrains the two endpoints by pattern property, so the explicit `all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.scope = $scope)` on line 56 is doing the real work of stopping a path from walking through another tenant's nodes mid-hop. If that line were ever dropped in a refactor, the endpoint check alone would silently let cross-scope data leak into results.

The budget-aware evidence loop is doing more than one job at once: it decides whether a path's 'why' text fits the byte budget, but regardless of that decision it still adds the path's nodes/edges to the graph block. That means the returned graph can show relationships that have no cited evidence behind them once the budget is exceeded — worth confirming that's intentional.
stop-1.rationale: A single hunk combines security-sensitive scope filtering, a ranking heuristic baked into raw Cypher, and budget-aware evidence assembly — each piece is readable alone but their interactions are easy to get subtly wrong and hard to verify without a live database.

notes.title: The query: scope guard, hub damping, injected hop count
notes.body: Builds the Cypher string, validating `hops` as an integer in range before splicing it in (the only place raw interpolation happens — everything else is parameterised, so no injection risk there). The seed is scope- and stub-checked; paths are expanded undirected up to `hops`; every node and relationship on the path is re-checked against `$scope`/`$minConfidence`/`$rels`; rank is confidence-product divided by log(degree) to damp hub nodes; results are capped at `$paths` per seed before being returned as nested maps.
notes.concern: `all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE n.scope = $scope)` on line 56 is the only thing stopping a path from traversing through nodes outside the caller's scope — the `{scope: $scope}` pattern on `reached` alone only checks the endpoint. It's correct here but easy to lose in a future edit since it reads like a redundant check. Also, `COUNT { (reached)--() }` counts degree with no scope or confidence filter, so ranking can be skewed by relationships the caller would never actually see.

notes.title: Pruning: drop cyclic and subsumed paths after the fact
notes.body: `matchesOf` turns raw rows into `Match`es, first dropping any path that visits the same node twice (`simple`), then dropping any path that's a strict prefix of a longer one (`extendsPath`), then keeping only the top `PATHS_PER_MATCH`. This is the client-side half of the pruning story the Cypher query doesn't do itself.
notes.concern: The Cypher `[0..$paths]` slice happens *before* this duplicate-node filtering, so a cyclic/non-simple path can occupy one of the limited slots the DB sends back, pushing out a legitimate simple path that would have made the final cut. The fix (filtering duplicates in Cypher too) looks possible but wasn't done — likely fine in practice since bidirectional cycles should rank poorly, but it's an assumption, not a guarantee.

notes.title: Rendering a path as a sentence, and as a search hit
notes.body: `describePath` walks nodes in order and infers arrow direction by comparing each edge's stored `target` to the current node — correct because Neo4j relationships always carry a fixed direction regardless of how the pattern was matched. `hitOf` turns a match into a `SearchHit`, falling back from content to title for the excerpt and only attaching `detail`/`passage`/`revision` when non-empty.

notes.title: Assembling the answer: budget-bounded evidence, unbounded graph
notes.body: Walks every shown match's paths, turning each into a 'derived-fact' evidence item if it fits `maxEvidenceBytes` (tracked via a running `used` byte count), while always adding the path's nodes/edges to the graph maps regardless of whether the evidence was kept. Edges are deduped by a `source\0rel\0target` key, accumulating `evidenceIds` from every path that uses them. The graph block is spliced in right after the first (entities) block of `answer.blocks`.
notes.concern: Once the evidence budget is exhausted, later paths still contribute nodes and edges to the graph with no `evidenceIds`, so the returned graph can contain relationships without any citation backing them. If that's not intended, nodes/edges should be skipped (or clearly flagged) once `truncated` is set. Separately, splicing after `answer.blocks[0]` assumes `searchAnswer` always puts entities first — not checked here, just relied on.

alternatives.title: Keep ranking/hub-damping in Cypher as-is (current approach)
alternatives.pros: One round trip, server does the heavy lifting, avoids pulling the whole neighbourhood over the wire just to rank it in JS.
alternatives.cons: The ranking formula and scope-safety logic live in a hand-built string that can only really be proven right against a live Neo4j instance — unit tests on `matchesOf`/`subgraphAnswer` can't catch a mistake in the Cypher itself.

alternatives.title: Fetch raw candidate paths, do ranking/damping/pruning in TypeScript
alternatives.pros: Ranking logic becomes pure-function testable without a database; easier to reason about and adjust without touching Cypher.
alternatives.cons: Needs the query to return more paths per seed (to leave room for post-hoc pruning), more data over the wire, and duplicates logic that's naturally expressed as `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` in the database.

stop-1.pick: I'd keep the ranking in Cypher as this PR does — it's the right trade-off for a single round-trip design — but I'd want to see the scope-guard line (56) called out with a comment explaining it's not redundant, since it's the one line standing between this query and a cross-tenant data leak.
questions: Where is `$paths` set (presumably `2 * PATHS_PER_MATCH` per the docstring), and is that relationship enforced anywhere or just a comment someone could drift from?

Is it intentional that nodes/edges still get added to the graph block (lines 229-253) for paths whose evidence was dropped once the byte budget is hit, leaving uncited relationships in the returned graph?

take: This stop is the wiring: the adapter now calls one `subgraph-search.ts` function instead of full-text-then-per-hit-neighbours, and the actual ranking/traversal/damping logic (Match, hitOf, matchesOf, subgraphQuery) lives in a module not shown in this diff. So most of what's reviewable here is plumbing — but two pieces of real logic snuck in: the `answer()` deadline handling got reworked to recompute remaining time after the Cypher-fallback attempt, and the user-facing `assumptions` text now describes the traversal/damping algorithm in prose that has to stay in sync with code we can't see here.

The N+1 elimination is confirmed by deletion: `neighbours()` (the old per-hit 1-hop query) is gone, and `read()`/`rowsOf()` are pulled out as shared helpers used by both the Cypher port and the new subgraph path — solid dedup.

One quiet behavior change: `search()`'s full-text fallback previously ran via `run()`/`executeQuery` with no explicit timeout; now it runs via `read()` with `CYPHER_TIMEOUT_MS` enforced. That's probably right, but it's a behavior change riding along in a 'just wiring' stop.
stop-2.rationale: Mostly mechanical replacement of one query path with another, but the deadline-recompute logic and the user-facing description of ranking/damping are real correctness/maintainability surface area, even though the heavy algorithm lives in a file not in this diff.

notes.title: Logic moves out to subgraph-search.ts
notes.body: Swaps imports for `describeNeighbours`/`relevantExcerpt`/`searchAnswer` for `subgraphAnswer`/`subgraphQuery`/`matchesOf`/`hitOf`/`Traversal`. Confirms this stop is pure delegation — the actual ranking, path-selection, and excerpt logic now lives in `subgraph-search.ts`, which isn't part of this diff.
notes.concern: Can't assess correctness of the new ranking/damping logic from this stop alone; it's entirely trusted from here.

notes.title: New `traversal` config merged with defaults
notes.body: `this.traversal = { ...DEFAULT_TRAVERSAL, ...config.traverse }` — adds a new adapter config surface (`hops`, `minConfidence`, `rels`) that controls the subgraph query's shape. Reasonable way to make the traversal tunable without a schema migration.

notes.title: Deadline recomputed after the Cypher-fallback attempt, and ranking prose embedded in the answer
notes.body: `timeLeft()` is now a closure called twice: once up front, once after the (possibly slow) Cypher-generation attempt, so the subgraph query gets however much budget is actually left rather than a stale estimate from the start of `answer()`. That's a real correctness fix for deadline accounting. Separately, the `reach`/`assumptions` strings now describe the traversal depth, confidence filter, relationship filter, and the path-ranking formula (confidence product, damped by well-connectedness) in prose that ships to the caller as part of the answer.
notes.concern: The prose assumptions describe an algorithm that lives in `subgraph-search.ts` — if that file's ranking formula changes, this string has to be updated by hand and nothing will flag the drift. Also: `timeLeft()` can throw mid-`answer()` after diagnostics have already been pushed, discarding them — same as the old single check, but now it can trigger later in the flow, after a possibly expensive Cypher attempt.

notes.title: Single subgraph query replaces full-text + per-hit neighbour query
notes.body: Builds params (`lucene`, `scope`, `matches`, `paths`, `minConfidence`, `rels`) and runs one `subgraphQuery(hops)` through the new shared `read()` helper, then hands raw rows to `matchesOf()`. This is the actual N+1 elimination the PR title promises.
notes.concern: `paths: neo4j.int(PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2)` fetches twice as many paths as are ultimately kept (`PATHS_PER_MATCH`). That buffer factor is unexplained here — presumably `matchesOf` or `subgraphQuery` dedups/filters down, but the `*2` is a magic number with no comment pointing at why 2 and not some other factor.

notes.title: `neighbours()` deleted; `read()`/`rowsOf()` extracted and shared
notes.body: The old per-hit 1-hop neighbour query is gone entirely, confirming the N+1 elimination. `read()` (session + timeout) and `rowsOf()` (Neo4j Integer coercion) are pulled out and now shared between `cypherPort().read` and the new `subgraphSearch`, removing duplicated session-handling code.

alternatives.title: Batch the neighbour lookups with one UNWIND query instead of one combined full-text+traversal query
alternatives.pros: Keeps full-text ranking and graph-traversal/damping as two separably testable concerns; still only 2 round trips instead of 1+N; smaller behavioral surface change from the original code.
alternatives.cons: Still two queries, not one; doesn't get the single-query ranking-across-everything property this PR is going for, and the PR title specifically promises 'one native query.'

alternatives.title: Push the path-ranking/damping into an APOC path-expansion procedure instead of hand-written Cypher
alternatives.pros: Leverages a tested graph algorithm library rather than custom confidence-weighted damping logic buried in a Cypher string.
alternatives.cons: Adds an APOC dependency and deployment complexity; less portable across Neo4j editions/hosts.

stop-2.pick: I'd keep the single native query as implemented — it genuinely removes the N+1 and lets ranking span the whole match+path space in one go, which the two-query alternative can't do as cleanly. The main cost is that the ranking/damping logic is now Cypher-embedded and hard to unit-test outside the database, so I'd want to see that logic's tests before trusting the prose in the `assumptions` string.
questions: Where is `subgraph-search.ts` (the module with `matchesOf`, `hitOf`, `subgraphQuery`, the damping formula) tested — is there a unit test for the ranking logic independent of a live Neo4j instance?
Is `PATHS_PER_MATCH * 2` a tuned constant with a reason, or just a safety buffer — should it be named or documented?

take: This is a small schema addition: a `traverse` config block with three optional knobs (`hops`, `minConfidence`, `rels`) that presumably get read in `subgraph-search.ts` to build the Cypher expansion. The validation itself is straightforward zod — bounded ints, bounded floats, non-empty string arrays.

The thing to watch is that the comment documents defaults (`hops` default 2, `minConfidence` default 0) but the schema has no `.default()` calls — all three fields are just `.optional()`. That means the actual defaulting behavior lives entirely in the consuming code, not here, so this file alone can't be trusted to know what happens when `traverse` is omitted.
Nothing about this hunk is risky on its own; it's just config shape. The interesting correctness question is downstream, in how `MAX_HOPS` and the traverse fields get consumed.
stop-3.rationale: It's an additive zod schema with bounded primitives and a constant — no branching logic, no state, no I/O.

notes.title: New MAX_HOPS constant
notes.body: Caps hop count at 3, with a one-line rationale (diminishing returns past 3 hops). Used both as the upper bound in the schema below and presumably as a ceiling/default in the query builder.

notes.title: New `traverse` config block
notes.body: Adds an optional `traverse` object with `hops` (1-3), `minConfidence` (0-1), and `rels` (non-empty string array) — the knobs that will shape the generated Cypher's expansion depth, relationship confidence filter, and relationship-type filter.
notes.concern: The doc comment states defaults (hops=2, minConfidence=0) but none of these fields use `.default()` in the schema — so parsing an omitted `traverse` just gives `undefined`, not the documented defaults. Anyone reading only this file would think the schema guarantees the defaults; it doesn't, they must be applied in the consumer. Worth confirming that's intentional and that `subgraph-search.ts` actually applies them consistently.

alternatives.title: Apply `.default()` in the schema itself
alternatives.pros: Defaults live in one place, next to their documentation; consumers can rely on `hops`/`minConfidence` always being defined after parsing.
alternatives.cons: Slightly more code here, and makes the parsed config shape diverge from the authored config shape (annoying if you ever need to tell 'user didn't set this' from 'user set it to the default').

alternatives.title: Keep defaults purely in the consumer (current approach)
alternatives.pros: Schema stays a pure validation boundary; defaulting logic sits next to where it's used, which can make the query-building code self-contained and easier to test in isolation.
alternatives.cons: Risk of the comment here and the actual default value drifting apart over time, since nothing enforces they match.

stop-3.pick: I'd keep defaulting in the consumer as done here, but I'd want to see the default applied in exactly one place in `subgraph-search.ts` (not re-derived in multiple spots) so the comment here stays truthful.
questions: Where exactly do the default `hops=2` and `minConfidence=0` get applied — once, or wherever `traverse` is read?
Is there a test asserting that an omitted `traverse` config produces the documented defaults end-to-end?
